recipe.history:
Mushrooms occupy a singular position in the human culinary record — neither plant nor animal, the fungi kingdom represents a kingdom unto itself, and humans have been harvesting and eating wild mushrooms for as long as we have evidence of human foraging behavior. The ancient Egyptians considered mushrooms a food reserved for royalty, believing they sprang from lightning and were therefore divine. Greek and Roman writers documented culinary and medicinal uses of several mushroom species. In East Asia, the cultivation of mushrooms — particularly shiitake, maitake, and enoki — has been practiced for at least two thousand years, with Chinese texts from the Han dynasty describing shiitake cultivation techniques still broadly recognizable today. Europe developed a rich tradition of wild mushroom foraging, particularly in France, Italy, Poland, and Russia, where porcini, chanterelle, morel, and black truffle defined the highest registers of local cuisines. The common white button mushroom, Agaricus bisporus, which accounts for the majority of commercially grown mushrooms worldwide, was first cultivated in France in the 17th century and arrived in American commercial agriculture in the late 19th century, eventually becoming so ubiquitous that for much of the 20th century 'mushroom' in American cooking meant almost exclusively this one species.

The mushroom's journey from a single-species American ingredient to the diverse, culinarily serious category it occupies today mirrors the broader gourmet food movement of the late 20th century. Specialty grocery stores, Asian markets, and the explosion of farmers markets in the 1980s and 1990s introduced American cooks to cremini, portobello, oyster, maitake, shiitake, king trumpet, and eventually more exotic varieties like lion's mane and hen-of-the-woods. On the burger, mushrooms took two distinct paths: the sautéed mushroom topping — cooked down in butter and thyme until collapsed and intensely savory — became a cornerstone of the 'steakhouse burger' style, while the portobello mushroom cap emerged in the 1990s as a vegetarian burger alternative. The umami depth of a well-cooked mixed mushroom blend, with its glutamate richness and meaty texture, makes it one of the most compelling toppings in the burger repertoire — a topping that amplifies rather than distracts from the beef beneath it.

I went through a mushroom phase in my late twenties that I can only describe as a religious conversion. I had grown up eating the canned cream-of-mushroom-soup style of mushroom preparation, which shares almost nothing with an actual mushroom except a vague brown color. Then I went to a farmers market on a whim one Saturday morning and a vendor handed me a piece of fresh sautéed hen-of-the-woods mushroom, cooked in nothing but butter and salt, and my understanding of what food could taste like shifted permanently. I bought every variety at the stall and went home and spent the afternoon cooking mushrooms in every combination I could think of. The mixed mushroom burger was born that day, though it took a few more iterations to arrive at the version that felt complete. A mixture of cremini, shiitake, and oyster mushrooms, cooked long and slow until their water releases and evaporates and they become concentrated and almost jammy in texture — that is the platonic ideal, and I have not deviated from it since.

A burger topped with deeply sautéed mixed mushrooms is, of all burgers, the one that most demands a properly cooked medium rare interior. The mushrooms bring enormous umami depth — glutamates from the fungi amplify the savory character of the beef in a way that no other topping quite replicates. But this amplification only works if the beef has something to give in return. A properly medium rare patty, cooked to 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, is giving everything it has: juices intact, fat rendered and fluid, the proteins firm enough to provide structure but not so contracted as to squeeze out flavor. The mushrooms rest on top of this and together they create a savory depth that is genuinely greater than the sum of its parts. Overcook the burger and the mushrooms, for all their glutamate richness, are providing depth to something that has nothing left to give. The interaction fails. The temperature is not a suggestion. It is the chemistry.
ingredients: Kosher salt and cracked black pepper
4 oz shiitake mushrooms, stems removed, caps sliced
4 oz oyster mushrooms, torn into pieces
1/4 cup dry white wine or dry sherry
2 tbsp fresh flat-leaf parsley, chopped (for finishing)
instructions: 1. Make the potato buns: Dissolve yeast in warm potato water with 1 tsp sugar, 5–7 minutes until foamy. Combine flour, sugar, and salt in stand mixer with dough hook.
2. Add mashed potato, yeast mixture, warm milk, and eggs. Mix on low until combined. Add softened butter in pieces. Knead on medium 8–10 minutes until smooth and slightly tacky.
3. Cover and let rise 1–1.5 hours until doubled. Divide into 6 portions, shape into rounds, place on parchment-lined baking sheets, and proof 45–60 minutes.
4. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash. Bake 15–17 minutes until golden brown. Cool on a rack.
5. Make the truffle aioli: Whisk together mayonnaise, truffle oil, lemon juice, grated garlic, and salt. Taste and adjust. Refrigerate until needed.

6. Cook the mixed mushrooms: Heat butter and olive oil in a large, wide skillet over medium-high heat. When the butter foams and subsides, add all mushrooms in a single layer (work in batches if needed). Do not stir for 3–4 minutes — let them develop a deep brown crust on one side.

7. Stir mushrooms and add shallots, garlic, thyme, and rosemary. Cook another 3–4 minutes, stirring occasionally. Add white wine and soy sauce; the liquid will sizzle and quickly reduce. Continue cooking until the mushrooms are deeply caramelized and any liquid has evaporated, 3–4 more minutes. Season with salt and pepper. Remove from heat and stir in fresh parsley. Keep warm.

8. Form patties: Gently combine chuck and sirloin. Divide into 4 portions (~6 oz each). Form into 3/4-inch thick patties with a thumb indent in the center. Season both sides with kosher salt and black pepper just before cooking.

9. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes on the first side without pressing. Flip, lay Gruyère slices on each, and cook 2–2.5 minutes more. Pull at 130–132°F and rest loosely foil-tented 3–4 minutes to reach 133–135°F.
10. Toast bun halves in butter until golden.

11. Assemble: Spread truffle aioli on both cut faces of each bun. Place butter lettuce on the bottom bun. Set the rested, cheese-topped patty on the lettuce. Spoon a generous mound of mixed mushroom sauté directly on top of the patty. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
